@graph.headline: How to Calculate Real Expectancy of a Trading Strategy (Gross vs Net, With the Indian Cost Stack)
@graph.description: Calculate real trading expectancy: the two-method cross-check, the Indian gross-vs-net cost stack, and the honesty-ledger rules that make the number real.

mainEntity.name: What is the formula for trading expectancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: (Win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss), with average loss entered as a positive magnitude. Or the shortcut: net profit ÷ number of closed trades, with breakevens and scratches counted as zero. Both give the same number — compute both and let them cross-check each other. The full journal build is Chapter 1's tutorial.

mainEntity.name: Should expectancy be calculated in rupees or in R?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both, for different jobs. ₹ answers "what does this pay me" — use it for P&L projections (net expectancy × realistic monthly frequency). R answers "how good is the strategy" — R-multiple comparisons travel across account sizes and position sizes, ₹ doesn't. Convert with: ₹ expectancy = R-expectancy × ₹ risk per trade.

mainEntity.name: What is a good expectancy for a trading system?

acceptedAnswer.text: The benchmark answer lives in Chapter 1's FAQ. The contract that matters more than the tier: whatever your number, know your n before you believe it.

mainEntity.name: How many trades do I need before my expectancy number is reliable?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under 30 trades is directional only; 30–100 is usable but noisy (watch the trend, not the point); 100+ is stable enough to size on. As a rule of thumb: an expectancy number without a sample size is a rumor. The full evidence contract is in the sample-size chapter.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between expectancy and profit factor?

acceptedAnswer.text: Profit factor (gross profit ÷ gross loss) is an efficiency ratio; expectancy (net profit ÷ trades) is money per trade. One lucky outlier can inflate profit factor while barely representing the system; expectancy spreads every trade's weight evenly across the count. They're linked by PF = p×R ÷ (1−p) — same ledger, different questions. The full treatment is in the profit factor chapter.

mainEntity.name: Do I subtract brokerage and taxes when calculating expectancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — this is the article's central move. Gross expectancy is the laboratory number; net expectancy (after brokerage, STT, exchange charges, stamp duty, SEBI fee, GST, plus slippage and spread) is the account's number. On a worked NIFTY option trade, the verified statutory round trip is ₹62.53 before slippage — and that fixed tax per trade can flip a thin +0.05R gross edge into a −0.03R net loss. Subtract costs as their own term; never fold them into the averages. One line on income tax: tax on F&O profits is computed annually on your net income and is NOT subtracted per trade — your per-trade net expectancy is what feeds the tax return, not the other way round.

mainEntity.name: How do I convert expectancy per trade into monthly income?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiply net per-trade expectancy by your realistic monthly trade frequency — realistic meaning after skipped signals and no-trade days, not the backtest's trade count. And remember the limit: the number says nothing about the path (drawdown) between here and the average.

mainEntity.name: Can a strategy have positive expectancy and still lose money?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, three ways: the sample was too small (variance), the costs weren't in the math (gross vs net), or the sequence hit a drawdown the account couldn't survive. Expectancy is an average — it is silent on the path.

mainEntity.name: What is expectancy ratio vs payoff ratio?

acceptedAnswer.text: A naming confusion worth clearing once: some pages call average win ÷ average loss the "expectancy ratio." It's the payoff ratio. Expectancy is the per-trade average in ₹ or R — never a ratio.
